title.en: Mixture of Experts: How Big Models Only Use a Slice of Themselves

description.en: Mistral Small 4 has 119B parameters but activates only 6B per token. The trick is Mixture of Experts — a router that picks the top few experts per token. Build the router and understand modern efficient LLMs.

story_variants.en:
## 119 Billion Parameters, but Only 6 Billion Do the Work

Vaathiyaar points at a spec sheet. "**Mistral Small 4**: 119 billion total parameters, but only **6 billion active** per token. How? It's not one giant network — it's a committee of specialists, and a **router** that calls only the right few for each word. This is **Mixture of Experts (MoE)**, and in 2026 it's how nearly every efficient frontier model is built."

### The Committee Model

Instead of running *all* parameters for *every* token, an MoE layer holds many small **experts** and a tiny **gate** (router). For each token the gate scores every expert, and only the **top-k** highest-scoring experts actually run. The rest stay asleep.

The payoff: the model has the *knowledge capacity* of 119B parameters, but the *compute cost* of only the few experts it wakes up. Big brain, small bill.

```
gate_scores = [0.1, 0.7, 0.2, 0.9]   # one score per expert
top_2 experts -> indices [3, 1]       # 0.9 and 0.7 win
```

### Why Top-K, Not All?

Running every expert would throw away the whole advantage — you'd pay for 119B every token. Running just the top-1 or top-2 keeps quality high while activating a tiny fraction. Choosing **k** is the core MoE trade-off: bigger k = smarter but slower.

> **Vaathiyaar's note:** when you read "119B total / 6B active," you're reading an MoE routing decision. The router you build today is the exact mechanism deciding which 6B wake up.

You'll implement `route(gate_scores, k)` — return the indices of the top-k experts, highest score first.

explanation.en: Order expert indices by their gate score, highest first
Wake only the top-k experts; the rest stay asleep (and free)

instruction.en: Implement `route(gate_scores, k)` — the MoE router. `gate_scores` is a list of one score per expert; return the **indices** of the top-k experts, highest score first. Then print `route([0.1, 0.7, 0.2, 0.9], 2)` (expected: `[3, 1]` — expert 3 scored 0.9, expert 1 scored 0.7).

q.en: Mistral Small 4 has 119B parameters but only 6B are 'active' per token. What does that mean?
q.ta: Mistral Small 4-இல் 119B அளவுருக்கள் உள்ளன, ஆனால் ஒரு டோக்கனுக்கு 6B மட்டுமே 'active'. இதன் பொருள் என்ன?

en: Each token runs all 119B, but only 6B are saved
Only the experts the router picks actually run for that token
The model was compressed down to 6B after training
Only 6B parameters were trained; the rest are random
ta: ஒவ்வொரு டோக்கனும் 119B முழுவதையும் இயக்கும், 6B மட்டுமே சேமிக்கப்படும்
அந்த டோக்கனுக்கு router தேர்ந்தெடுக்கும் experts மட்டுமே இயங்கும்

q.en:
What does this print?
s = [0.1, 0.7, 0.2, 0.9]
print(sorted(range(len(s)), key=lambda i: s[i], reverse=True)[:2])
q.ta:
இது என்ன அச்சிடும்?
s = [0.1, 0.7, 0.2, 0.9]
print(sorted(range(len(s)), key=lambda i: s[i], reverse=True)[:2])

en: reverse=True puts the lowest scores first
sorted() changes the original scores list
It returns the top scores, not the expert indices
[:k] returns k+1 items instead of k
ta: இது expert குறியீடுகளை அல்ல, அதிக மதிப்பெண்களைத் தருகிறது

q.en: In an MoE layer, what happens when you increase k (the number of experts picked per token)?
q.ta: ஒரு MoE அடுக்கில், k-ஐ (ஒரு டோக்கனுக்குத் தேர்ந்தெடுக்கும் experts எண்ணிக்கை) அதிகரித்தால் என்ன ஆகும்?

en: The model gains more total parameters
Nothing changes; only the router's speed changes
Quality tends to rise, but each token costs more compute
Compute per token drops because work is shared
ta: எதுவும் மாறாது; router-இன் வேகம் மட்டுமே மாறும்
தரம் உயரும், ஆனால் ஒவ்வொரு டோக்கனுக்கும் கணக்கீட்டுச் செலவு கூடும்
வேலை பகிரப்படுவதால் ஒரு டோக்கனுக்கான கணக்கீடு குறையும்
